outcomes.explain-nodes-and-links: Explain how nodes and links make up a linked list
outcomes.traverse-from-head: Traverse a linked list from its head with a pointer
outcomes.insert-in-constant-time: Insert a node at the head or after a known node in O(1)
outcomes.delete-by-relinking: Delete a node by relinking around it
outcomes.compare-with-arrays: Compare the costs of linked lists and arrays

the-problem.title: Adding to the front is expensive
the-problem.caption: Your task list is an array and a new task Z must go first. Every task that is already there has to shift one cell to the right to make room. With thousands of tasks, one insert moves thousands of cells.

a-node.title: A node holds a value and a next
a-node.caption: A linked list stores each item in its own node. A node holds two things: a value and a link called next. Here the single node holds A, and its next points nowhere yet.

linking-nodes.title: Nodes joined by links
linking-nodes.caption: You add B and C, then link A to B and B to C. The head tells you which node the list starts at. The last node's next is null, which means the list ends there.

traversal.title: Walking the list
traversal.caption: A pointer called current starts at the head. To move on, you follow the node's next link. This walk from node to node is called traversal.

insert-at-head.title: Insert at the head
insert-at-head.caption: You create node Z and link it to the old head, A. Then you make Z the new head. No other node is touched, however long the list is.

insert-after.title: Insert after a node
insert-after.caption: The pointer prev marks the node you insert after, and here it is A. You link the new node X to prev's next, B, first. Then you link prev to X, and the list stays whole.

delete-after.title: Delete by relinking
delete-after.caption: To delete X, you link prev to the node after X, which is B. Nothing points to X any more, so you can remove it. The rest of the list never moves.

access-by-index.title: Reaching an index takes a walk
access-by-index.caption: A list has no index to jump to. To reach index 3 you start at the head and follow next three times. Reaching index k takes k moves.

arrays-vs-lists.title: Arrays versus linked lists
arrays-vs-lists.caption: The array reads any index in one jump, but inserting at the front shifts every cell. The linked list inserts at the head in one step, but reaching a node means walking to it. Pick the structure that matches the operation you do most.

reverse-preview.title: Next up: reverse a list
reverse-preview.caption: In the Exercise you reverse a list in place with three pointers: prev, current and next. Before the first move, prev is null, current is at the head and next is one node ahead. You will redirect each node's link, one node at a time.

which-node-is-last.prompt: Select the last node of the list.
which-node-is-last.explanation: The last node is C because its next is null. Every other node's next points to a node.

where-current-moves.prompt: current is at B. Select the node it moves to next.
where-current-moves.explanation: current follows B's next link, which leads to C. It never jumps over a node or goes back, because links only point forward.

cost-of-insert-at-head.prompt: How much work does inserting at the head cost, as the list grows?

options.constant: O(1): a fixed number of link changes
options.shift-everything: O(n): every node has to move one place
options.walk-to-the-end: O(n): you must walk to the end first
options.halving: O(log n): the list is halved each time

cost-of-insert-at-head.explanation: It is O(1): one new node, one link and one head change, whatever the length. Nodes never shift, because a node's place is set by links rather than by position in memory. You also never walk to the end, since the head is already in hand. Nothing is halved, because nothing is searched.

first-link-to-change.prompt: You insert a node after prev. Which link do you set first?

options.new-to-next: The new node's next, to prev's current next
options.prev-to-new: prev's next, to the new node
options.either-order: Either order works, both links get set anyway
options.head-to-new: The head, to the new node

first-link-to-change.explanation: You set the new node's next first. If you link prev to the new node first, nothing points to B any more and B and C are lost. The order matters because prev's old next is the only reference to the rest of the list. The head belongs to insertion at the front, not after a node.

prev-next-after-deletion.prompt: X has been deleted. Select the node that prev's next points to now.
prev-next-after-deletion.explanation: prev's next points to B, the node that came after X. Relinking is what removes X, so prev does not point to X or end the list.

cost-of-reaching-index-k.prompt: What does reaching the node at index k cost in a linked list?

options.k-moves: k moves from the head, O(n) in the worst case
options.one-move: One move, O(1), like an array index
options.whole-list: n moves, because you always walk the whole list
options.halving: About log k moves, because you can skip nodes

cost-of-reaching-index-k.explanation: You follow k links from the head, so the cost grows with k and is O(n) in the worst case. A list cannot jump the way an array does, because nodes are not stored side by side. You stop at index k rather than at the end, and a link only leads to the next node, so there is nothing to skip.

linked-list.gloss: A chain of nodes where each node links to the next.

node.gloss: One item of a linked list: a value plus a link to the next node.

head.gloss: The first node of a linked list, where every traversal starts.

pointer.gloss: A labelled marker that refers to one node, like current or prev.

traversal.gloss: Visiting the nodes one after another by following their links.
